content: 1. Pharmacodynamic antagonism occurs when one drug reduces the effects of another. It is recommended to avoid or use an alternative drug in such cases. There is a potential risk of thromboembolic disorders, so close monitoring is advised. 2. Ribociclib can increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices by altering the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Caution should be exercised, and close monitoring is necessary. 3. Rifabutin decreases the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices by affecting the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Use caution and monitor closely. 4. Rifampin reduces the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices by influencing the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is required. 5. Rifapentine decreases the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices by altering the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Use caution and monitor closely. 6. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices by affecting the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. It is recommended to avoid or use an alternative drug. 7. St. John’s Wort reduces the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices by altering the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 8. Sugammadex sodium decreases the effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices through receptor binding competition. Avoid or use an alternative drug. In vitro binding studies suggest that sugammadex may bind to progestogen, reducing progestogen exposure. A bolus dose of sugammadex is considered equivalent to missing doses of hormonal contraceptives containing estrogen or progestogen. If an oral contraceptive is taken on the same day as sugammadex, or if the patient uses a transdermal or implant hormonal contraceptive, an additional nonhormonal contraceptive method (e.g., condoms and spermicides) should be used for the next 7 days. 9. Teriflunomide increases the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices through an unknown mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Tesamorelin decreases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices by altering metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 11. Topiramate reduces the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine devices by affecting the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 12. Patients with a personal or family history of venous thromboembolism (VTE), obesity, or systemic lupus erythematosus may have an increased risk of thromboembolic events. Estrogen therapy in postmenopausal women has been associated with a 2to 4-fold increase in the risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery. 13. Retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogens. Discontinue the medication if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia, or migraine. If examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions, estrogens should be discontinued. 14. Progestins combined with estrogens may pose additional risks compared to estrogen-alone regimens, including adverse effects on lipoprotein metabolism (e.g., lowering HDL, raising LDL) and impaired glucose tolerance. 15. In patients with pre-existing hypertriglyceridemia, estrogen therapy may elevate plasma triglycerides, potentially leading to pancreatitis and other complications. Discontinue therapy if pancreatitis occurs. 16. Observational studies have reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller increase in risk with estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use. Risks may persist for more than 10 years after discontinuation. A large meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies demonstrated that the risk is dependent on the duration of use. The Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) trials also showed an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy. 17. Estrogens may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function. Exercise caution in patients with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or pregnancy. Discontinue medication if jaundice recurs. 18. Patients dependent on thyroid hormone replacement therapy who are also receiving estrogens may require increased doses of thyroid replacement therapy. Thyroid function should be monitored to maintain free thyroid hormone levels within an acceptable range. 19. Use caution in individuals with severe hypocalcemia, as estrogen-induced hypocalcemia may occur in women with hypoparathyroidism. Consider whether the benefits of estrogen therapy outweigh the risks in such cases. 20. Exogenous estrogens may exacerbate symptoms of angioedema in women with hereditary angioedema. Assess whether the benefits of estrogen therapy outweigh the risks in these patients. 21. Estrogens are not indicated for use during pregnancy. Epidemiologic studies and meta-analyses have not shown an increased risk of genital or non-genital birth defects (including cardiac anomalies and limb-reduction defects) following exposure to combined hormonal contraceptives (estrogens and progestins) before conception or during early pregnancy. 22. Estrogens and progestogens are present in human milk and may reduce milk production in breastfeeding women. This reduction is less likely once breastfeeding is well-established. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered alongside the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child from treatment or the underlying maternal condition.
